verses.text: Moreover Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me now choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David tonight.
I will come on him while he is weary and exhausted, and will make him afraid. All the people who are with him will flee. I will strike the king only,
and I will bring back all the people to you. The man whom you seek is as if all returned. All the people shall be in peace.”
The saying pleased Absalom well, and all the elders of Israel.
Then Absalom said, “Now call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what he says.”
When Hushai had come to Absalom, Absalom spoke to him, saying, “Ahithophel has spoken like this. Shall we do what he says? If not, speak up.”
Hushai said to Absalom, “The counsel that Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai said moreover, “You know your father and his men, that they are mighty men, and they are fierce in their minds, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Your father is a man of war, and will not lodge with the people.

Behold, he is now hidden in some pit, or in some other place. It will happen, when some of them have fallen at the first, that whoever hears it will say, ‘There is a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom!’
Even he who is valiant, whose heart is as the heart of a lion, will utterly melt; for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and those who are with him are valiant men.
But I counsel that all Israel be gathered together to you, from Dan even to Beersheba, as the sand that is by the sea for multitude; and that you go to battle in your own person.

So shall we come on him in some place where he shall be found, and we will light on him as the dew falls on the ground; and of him and of all the men who are with him we will not leave so much as one.
Moreover, if he has gone into a city, then shall all Israel bring ropes to that city, and we will draw it into the river, until there isn’t one small stone found there.”

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” For Yahweh had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that Yahweh might bring evil on Absalom.
Then Hushai said to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, “Ahithophel counseled Absalom and the elders of Israel that way; and I have counseled this way.

Now therefore send quickly, and tell David, saying, ‘Don’t lodge tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over; lest the king be swallowed up, and all the people who are with him.’”
Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying by En Rogel; and a female servant used to go and tell them; and they went and told king David. For they might not be seen to come into the city.
But a boy saw them, and told Absalom. Then they both went away quickly, and came to the house of a man in Bahurim, who had a well in his court; and they went down there.
The woman took and spread the covering over the well’s mouth, and spread out bruised grain on it; and nothing was known.

Absalom’s servants came to the woman to the house; and they said, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” The woman said to them, “They have gone over the brook of water.” When they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.
After they had departed, they came up out of the well, and went and told king David; and they said to David, “Arise and pass quickly over the water; for thus has Ahithophel counseled against you.”
Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they passed over the Jordan. By the morning light there lacked not one of them who had not gone over the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey, arose, and went home, to his city, and set his house in order, and hanged himself; and he died, and was buried in the tomb of his father.
Then David came to Mahanaim. Absalom passed over the Jordan, he and all the men of Israel with him.
Absalom set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Now Amasa was the son of a man whose name was Ithra the Israelite, who went in to Abigail the daughter of Nahash, sister to Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
When David had come to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lodebar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim,
brought beds, basins, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, meal, parched grain, beans, lentils, roasted grain,
honey, butter, sheep, and cheese of the herd, for David, and for the people who were with him, to eat; for they said, “The people are hungry, and weary, and thirsty in the wilderness.”

footnotes.content: Ahithophel speaks with the confident voice of a man used to being heard. His counsel seems shrewd—catch David tired, strike decisively. But I've learned that plans wrought in haste, however clever, often miss what only the Lord can see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He maps it out like a man who knows war: find David weary, frighten his circle, let them scatter like sheep. How often do those who trust their own cunning forget that the throne belongs to God, not to whoever plans most perfectly?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahithophel promises peace through conquest—a quiet kingdom once David falls. Yet I wonder: what peace can come when it's built on ambition and blood rather than on the Lord's will? Absalom doesn't know it yet, but his 'all people in peace' will never settle his heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The counsel pleased Absalom and the elders—so often those in power surround themselves with voices that say what they want to hear. It's a loneliness disguised as agreement, and the young prince doesn't yet recognize it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom pauses. He wants another voice. It's a small, wise hesitation—Hushai waits in the wings, sent by David to be David's eyes. And I see in this moment how God sometimes gives us a chance to listen before we act, if we'll take it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom invites Hushai in and asks plainly: what do you make of Ahithophel's word? There's a courtesy here—he's still a son wanting counsel—but also a young man testing the room. Hushai has one chance to turn the son from destruction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hushai replies simply: not good counsel. Not this time. No flourish, just the truth spoken plainly. I've seen men save kingdoms with less—just a clear word at the threshold, before the gates close.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hushai speaks to what Absalom knows: your father is a man of war, fierce and cunning like a bear with cubs. He won't rest with the troops where Ahithophel expects him. Hushai reads David truly, and in that truth finds the flaw in Ahithophel's plan.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hushai plants a fear: when the first of your men fall in the dark—and they will—people will whisper that a great slaughter has begun. Rumor moves faster than truth, and Absalom's courage will crumble with his army's morale.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The bravest heart will melt when the report spreads, Hushai warns. For all Israel knows David's name—his strength, his men. What sounds like an easy victory will become, in the minds of soldiers, a suicide run. Fear is contagion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Instead, Hushai counsels: gather all Israel—from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south—and you yourself lead them. This touches Absalom's pride and flatters his ambition to march at the head of a nation united. It sounds grander, and it buys David time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: With such numbers, Hushai says, you'll find David like dew settling on ground—inevitable, total. Not a man escaped. The poetry of it appeals to young ambition, and the delay it requires means David runs deeper into safety.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he flees into a city, Hushai adds, all Israel will rope that city and drag it into the river until not a stone stands. It's hyperbole, yet it captures Absalom's vision of absolute dominion. Hushai has given the young rebel a grander dream than Ahithophel's, and dreams take time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The text tells it plainly: Absalom and all Israel agreed Hushai's counsel was better. But then it adds the hidden truth: Yahweh had ordained to defeat Ahithophel's counsel, so that He might bring calamity on Absalom. What looks like Hushai's cleverness is the Lord's hand, turning the heart of a son to his own undoing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Hushai moves quickly to the priests—Zadok and Abiathar. He must tell David what has been decided. The game has turned; the king's life hangs on a message carried in darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hushai's message is urgent: don't stay at the river fords. Cross now. The fords are where Absalom might cut off escape. One night's rest could cost David his life. Sometimes mercy speaks in haste.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan and Ahimaaz wait by En Rogel, hidden. A servant-woman carries their messages—the weak and the ordinary become the bridge between the court and the hunted king. God often works through those no one is watching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A boy sees them, and the men must run. They flee to a house in Bahurim where a well sits in the courtyard. One room, one hidden shaft into darkness—their salvation in a moment of exposure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The woman spreads grain over the well's mouth. It looks like nothing, like a day's work in the yard. But this small act of courage—a hidden hospitality—saves the messengers who save the king. Faithfulness doesn't announce itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom's men come searching. The woman tells them the men crossed the brook. It's a lie spoken calmly, and it works. They search the road that leads away and find nothing. A quick word saves a life—sometimes that's how the kingdom turns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once the hunters are gone, Jonathan and Ahimaaz climb up from the well and run to David with their message. They've seen the machinery of conspiracy and lived to tell it. The king now knows Hushai has bought him time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David rises and his people cross the Jordan. By morning, not one soul remains on the far side. It's the speed of grace—a man and a nation given breath when breath was almost gone. The river separates the hunted from the hunter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahithophel sees his counsel rejected. He saddles his donkey, goes home, sets his house in order, and takes his own life. His wisdom failed him; pride could not endure it. A man's brilliance means nothing if it serves a cause the Lord will not support.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David reaches Mahanaim, a place of safety and rest. Absalom and his army cross the Jordan in pursuit—the rebel king now on David's side of the river, but too late to catch him. Distance and time have shifted the odds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom sets Amasa as commander in place of Joab—his uncle, the son of Ithra. He gathers commanders loyal to the rebellion, building a court of his own. Yet every move binds him tighter to a cause God has already decided against.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom and his host camp in Gilead, marshaling their forces. The rebel army looks strong—well-fed, growing larger. But David is already building too, gathering strength from those who know his name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now comes the turn: Shobi of Rabbah, Machir of Lodebar, Barzillai of Rogelim—men who could have stayed silent—come to David with food and care. Even in exile, the king finds friends. Faithfulness recognizes faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bring beds, basins, wheat, barley, beans, lentils, roasted grain. The offering is plain and generous—what people can spare from the land. It's not royal feasting, but something more precious: the care of those who stand with you when standing costs something.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They say to David: 'The people are hungry, weary, thirsty in the wilderness.' Readers today hear an echo in those words—how often the Lord's people are weak and spent, yet find kindness in unexpected places. He provides not always in grandeur, but through the faithful few who see a need and act.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
